name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
description: POPE is a polling-based object probing evaluation benchmark for assessing object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about objects in images (e.g., 'Is there a car in the image?'). The dataset is built on MSCOCO validation images and supports three sampling strategies: Random, Popular, and Adversarial. It also supports automatic annotation via segmentation tools like SEEM for unannotated datasets.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
publisher: Renmin University of China, Meituan Group
citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3, 2023.
rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset is constructed from the MSCOCO validation set. 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in annotations are randomly selected for POPE evaluation. For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions are sampled from the MSCOCO validation set. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or via automatic segmentation using SEEM. Negative (nonexistent) objects are sampled using three strategies: Random, Popular, and Adversarial.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: MSCOCO (Microsoft Common Objects in Context) validation set, including human annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions. Additional datasets used include A-OKVQA and GQA, annotated using the SEEM automatic segmentation tool.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative object sampling strategies are applied: (1) Random Sampling: randomly sample objects not present in the image; (2) Popular Sampling: select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that do not exist in the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling: rank objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k frequent ones not present in the image. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set to 1:1 for label balance. Six questions are constructed per image (l=6).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For CHAIR evaluation, only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge are considered, following Rohrbach et al. (2018). For POPE, images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are selected. For SEEM-based POPE, automatic segmentation is applied to annotate objects in unannotated datasets. ChatGPT is used to parse open-ended LVLM responses for VQA evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object annotations are taken from existing MSCOCO human annotations. For unannotated datasets (A-OKVQA, GQA), automatic segmentation using SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) is used to generate object annotations. Polling questions are formulated using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?' with binary Yes/No answers.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic segmentation-based annotation
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The consistency between SEEM-based annotations and human annotations was analyzed. A performance gap was observed between annotation-based and SEEM-based POPE (e.g., F1 Score 71.37 vs. 62.70 for MiniGPT-4 under Adversarial setting), attributed to finer granularity of SEEM segmentation results. Consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and model-generated captions was also validated: out of 1303 and 1445 objects given 'No' responses by InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4, merely 0 and 5 were referenced in captions.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image (3 ground-truth objects and 3 nonexistent objects, ratio 1:1)
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic object segmentation and annotation; ChatGPT for parsing open-ended LVLM responses in VQA evaluation
rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world applications. For example, an autonomous driving system with incorrect understanding of the external environment could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The work also highlights risks for blind users relying on computer-generated captions of images.
rai:dataBiases: Visual instruction datasets used to train LVLMs (mostly constructed based on MSCOCO) have an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the instruction data. Approximately half of hallucinated objects in each image belong to the top 10 frequently appearing COCO objects.
rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation focuses only on coarse-grained object hallucination and does not consider fine-grained hallucinations such as object number, attributes, and positions. Evaluation is conducted on a subset of the validation set due to computation resource limitations, which may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide explicit Yes/No answers, leading to inaccurate evaluation. When combined with automatic segmentation tools, annotated objects may be inconsistent with human annotations. Only a small number of LVLMs are compared, excluding some recently released or closed-source models.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in large vision-language models. The dataset supports benchmarking LVLMs on hallucination under three difficulty settings (Random, Popular, Adversarial). It can also be extended to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation tools for scalable evaluation.
